activities.anchor: the treaty's greatest cost was not measured in gold marks
activities.caption: bet before you read on — the real bill
activities.name: toeLegitPredict

config.q: The page's opening thesis names one cost bigger than the reparations bill. Which one?
choices: In territory — Germany lost about 13 per cent of its land
In legitimacy — the Germans who had to live under it were never allowed to agree with it
In dollars — the settlement rested on American loans
config.why: A peace the defeated hate is a debt the future pays — the legitimacy gap is why every later crisis could be hung around Versailles's neck.

activities.caption: pair each setting detail with its meaning
activities.name: toeSettingMatch

config.prompt: Paris, 1919 — pair each detail with what it signalled:

pairs.right: deliberately the anniversary of the German Empire's proclamation at Versailles, 1871
Wilson, Clemenceau, Lloyd George — and Italy's Orlando, who mattered least
mid-civil-war, and not invited at all
a million names on petitions from every borderland in Europe

config.why: Six months of conference under enormous pressure: empires collapsing across Europe, revolution in the air — and Germany not invited to negotiate.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the three mandates
activities.name: toeAimsSpot

config.prompt: One line of this summary of the Big Three is wrong — click it:
lines: Wilson: the Fourteen Points — open diplomacy, self-determination, a League of Nations.
Clemenceau: France invaded twice, about 1.3 million dead — Germany disarmed, made to pay, pinned down.
Lloyd George: 'squeeze the German lemon till the pips squeak' in public; a middle peace in private.
Each answered to a different public: a Congress, a parliament, a victorious electorate.
Yet none of the three answered to anyone, so the compromise was free.
config.correction: Each answered to a public with its own arithmetic — the compromise was constrained before the first session began.
config.why: Wilson to a Congress that would vote his peace down, Clemenceau to a parliament that nearly toppled him for being too soft, Lloyd George to an electorate drunk on victory: judging the treaty means judging 1919's politics.

activities.caption: drag the divider — promised, then delivered
activities.name: toeResidueCompare

config.prompt: What the victors promised themselves, and what the residue kept — drag the divider:

before.label: The promises, 1919
before.text: Self-determination as the peace's foundation; an Anglo-American guarantee of French security; a Germany squeezed till the pips squeak.

after.label: The residue, 1920–22
after.text: Self-determination for the enemies' empires only; the guarantee dead in Washington; a German fleet scuttled at Scapa Flow — and its author privately calling the treaty a mistake.

config.why: When everyone feels robbed, the settlement has no constituency for defending it — Italy's 'mutilated victory', China refusing to sign at all.

activities.anchor: fixed by the London Schedule of May 1921
activities.caption: call the bill — the London Schedule
activities.name: toeTermsEstimate

config.prompt: Reparations were fixed in 1921 at 132 billion gold marks — roughly how many pounds sterling?
config.why: About £6.6 billion — billed to a power legally responsible under Article 231, the war guilt clause: less a moral verdict than a legal hinge that made the bill enforceable.

activities.caption: place the share — the map shrinks
activities.name: toeTermsPlace

config.prompt: In all, Germany lost what share of its population under the new borders?
config.why: A tenth of its people — with about 13 per cent of the land and nearly half its iron-ore reserves: Alsace-Lorraine to France, the Polish Corridor cutting East Prussia off, Danzig a free city, the Saar run by the League for fifteen years.

activities.caption: line up the crisis chain, earliest first
activities.name: toeCrisisOrder

config.prompt: Germany under the treaty — order the chain, earliest first:
items: The Kapp Putsch: right-wing veterans seize Berlin, defeated by a general strike — March 1920
Foreign minister Rathenau machine-gunned in the street — 1921
Coal deliveries missed; French and Belgian troops occupy the Ruhr — January 1923
Passive resistance paid for by printing money — 1923
One US dollar buys 4.2 trillion marks; the Rentenmark stops the freefall — November 1923
config.why: The treaty's economics turned physical: each event feeds the next — the chain a consequences question asks you to reconstruct. The Dawes Plan (1924) then stabilised it all on American credit that died with Wall Street in 1929.

config.root: Paris, mid-1919. You are a newspaper judging the treaty with contemporary eyes only — no hindsight allowed. Which case do you print?

start.text: The terms are on the table. Your verdict?

choices.label: Print the prosecuting case
choices.feedback: Brest-Litovsk was far harsher; northern France lies in ruins; Belgium was invaded.

choices.label: Print the defending case
choices.feedback: Keynes warns of a Carthaginian peace; Foch counts twenty years.

choices.label: Split the verdict: terms, not process
choices.feedback: The clauses may be defensible — a dictated signature and a war-guilt insult are not.

prosecute.text: Germany's outrage looks selective: at Brest-Litovsk in March 1918 it imposed on Russia a peace taking about a third of its population and most of its industry. Northern France really lies in ruins — mines flooded, towns razed — and a power that had shot civilians en route has little standing to complain of severity.

defend.text: Keynes, quitting the British delegation, publishes The Economic Consequences of the Peace within six months, warning of a 'Carthaginian peace'; Marshal Foch calls the treaty 'an armistice for twenty years' — and many French think it too soft, since Germany remains intact.

split.text: Content versus form: the terms are arguably defensible against a power that started — or at minimum lost — the war, but a dictated signature and a war-guilt clause that reads as an insult ensure they are never accepted as legitimate.

config.why: Versailles failed less as a bill than as a settlement — the deepest judgement distinguishes content from form.
